To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a simple cubic fit to a temperature-dependent opacity change, with coefficients that are functions of the logarithm to base 10 of the temperature, provides a good representation of the opacity change required, that the change is largest close to the base and smallest in the solar core and that the change is not physically realistic.

a 30% increase in opacity in a solar model with a revised composition is sufficient to bring it into agreement with helioseismology, and that the required opacity change can be represented as a simple cubic in the logarithm of the temperature.
the revised solar models are in better agreement with helioseismology if the opacity is increased by 30 per cent at the base of the solar convection zone and by a few percent in deeper layers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the opacity change that would be required to compensate for a change in the solar composition.
the question of the physical realism of the opacity changes required by the new composition, and we conclude that it is not.
the effect of the revised solar composition on the solar models and the effect of the opacity change required for the revised models to be consistent with helioseismology.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the solar models with the revised composition can only be made to match the solar sound-speed profile with a significant opacity change.
the opacity change required is not implausible and that the opacity change is not implausible.
the opacity is still not well known and that the solar sound-speed profile cannot be used as a test for it.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the opacity change required is not unreasonable but is still larger than the uncertainty on the opacity in this regime.
the opacity change required by the new solar composition is of similar magnitude to those that have been inferred from the helioseismic sound-speed differences.
the opacity change required is not physically plausible.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a change in the solar sound-speed profile of the magnitude that would reconcile the models and helioseismic data can be obtained with a relatively modest change in opacity.
a change in opacity can be used to compensate for a revised composition, and thus the problem can be reformulated as one in which the opacity and composition are simultaneously determined.
the opacity increase required to compensate for changes in the solar composition is small.
